subtitle: Learn plain meanings for twelve terms used in People, Access and Culture work, from civil rights and fair treatment to language access and person-centered practice, and use each one to frame a clear work question.
scope: For staff across DHS who want clear meanings for the terms used in People, Access and Culture work and want to connect them to a concrete task. This is a learning glossary with practice cases, not a legal finding, accommodation decision or cultural assessment. Civil rights duties, required policies and authorized procedures stay with the person or area responsible.
introTranscript: Words like access, fair treatment and civil rights help when they point to a specific part of the work. This course gives twelve common terms a plain meaning through a DHS team preparing a community meeting about a renewal notice. You will separate who attends from whose input can shape a decision, a difference in results from its explanation, general access from an individual accommodation, and a cultural habit from a civil rights duty such as language access. You will also turn a broad goal into a clear note that someone can act on and check. The aim is to use the words accurately, apply the same fair process to everyone, and never ask anyone to disclose personal information.

lessons.title: Start with the decision, then the word
lessons.summary: Connect a broad term to a concrete work question and the civil rights duties behind it.
lessons.objective: Explain how People, Access and Culture terms connect to existing civil rights duties and fair process.
objectives: Explain how People, Access and Culture terms connect to existing civil rights duties and fair process.
Identify which part of a task a broad term describes.
Rewrite a broad statement as a question that can be checked.
takeaways: A term is useful when it names a specific part of the work.
Civil rights laws already set duties for fair treatment, access and language access.
Asking what a word means is a fair question, not resistance.
lessons.statement: Name the work question before relying on the label.

image.caption: Two colleagues point to a line in a printed document they are reviewing together.

intro.heading: The words should make the work clearer
intro.body:
This course uses People, Access and Culture as the name for work on fair treatment, usable access and respectful service across cultures. Much of that work rests on duties that already exist in law. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act bars discrimination based on race, color or national origin in federally funded programs. Title VII covers employment. The Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act cover disability. The Minnesota Human Rights Act adds state protections.

Words in this area help only when they point to a specific part of the work. Consider a DHS team led by Rosa that is preparing a community meeting about a change to a renewal notice. Malik says the meeting should be more welcoming. That is a fair concern, but it is not yet a task. Does he mean the invitation list, the reading level of the notice, the location, interpreters, or whether comments can still change the draft? Each of those needs different evidence.

Clarifying a term should make it easier to take part, not test what someone knows. A respectful question asks which part of the meeting needs attention and what happened there. Do not assume that a person who asks for a definition opposes the purpose. People can understand the subject well and still use different words.

This course gives twelve terms a plain meaning: access, accommodation, language access, plain language, fair treatment, civil rights, disparity, equity as the DHS Equity Policy uses it, inclusion as belonging, culture, intercultural skill and person-centered practice. A definition helps organize thinking. It does not decide a legal question. When a formal duty is involved, use the written policy and the person or area responsible.

inThisLesson: Connect the terms to civil rights duties.
Find the task behind a broad word.
lessons.keyStatement: Clear words support understanding; they should never become a gate people must pass to take part.

flashcards.back: Legal protections against discrimination, such as Title VI and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, Section 504 and the Minnesota Human Rights Act.
Applying the same relevant standards to everyone, and removing barriers through accommodation and language access, without preferring or excluding anyone because of a protected trait.
The task, decision or situation in which a word is used.
A specific issue that can be checked with evidence and with the views of the people affected.

items.title: Specific meaning
items.body: Ask what part of the meeting the word welcoming describes. An invitation list, a readable notice and a chance to change the draft are different parts of the process. Naming the part turns the concern into something the team can act on.

items.title: Different understandings
items.body: People use one word for different experiences. Summarize what you heard and invite correction. The task and its effect matter more than technical vocabulary.

items.title: Named legal duties
items.body: A civil rights duty carries requirements that a general definition does not capture. Title VI, the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Minnesota Human Rights Act each have their own scope. Keep the actual requirement and use its procedure through the person or area responsible.

tabs.label: Broad label
tabs.body: “The meeting is welcoming” states a conclusion without the supporting account. Ask who could attend, who could understand the materials and how comments were used. The label alone does not show anyone’s experience.

tabs.label: Concrete question
tabs.body: “Could people who read Spanish or Somali get the notice before the meeting, and could written comments reach Rosa before the draft closed?” This names conditions the team can check. It asks nothing about anyone’s identity or beliefs.

tabs.label: Vocabulary test
tabs.body: Requiring people to define every term before they speak adds a barrier. Explain the word that matters and look at the concern. A question about meaning usually improves shared understanding.

check.question: Malik says the meeting should be “more welcoming.” What is the most useful response?
check.correct: Ask which part of the meeting needs attention and what he saw that raised the concern.
wrong: Treat the phrase as proof that the whole process has failed.
Ask Malik to define every related term before the team discusses it.
Assume the comment is a complaint about Rosa’s leadership.
check.feedbackCorrect: This links the broad word to a specific condition the team can check. It also treats Malik’s concern as useful information.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A broad phrase does not prove a failure or reveal a motive, and a vocabulary test does not improve access. Ask about the task, the concern and what was observed before choosing a response.

sorting.heading: Term in context, work question or unsupported judgment?

items.text: Language access concerns whether people with limited English can understand the notice and the meeting.
Fair treatment means the same comment deadline and review steps apply to every commenter.
Did the translated notice reach readers before the comment period opened?
Which meeting materials could not be opened with a screen reader?
Asking what a word means shows the person does not care.
Putting the word welcoming in the invitation proves the meeting was welcoming.

lessons.next: Next, look at inclusion as belonging: who is present and whose input can shape the work.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Dana asks what “inclusive” means for the renewal notice meeting. A colleague replies that the question shows Dana is not on board.
options: Explain the participation question the word points to and ask Dana what she has noticed.
Ask Dana to explain her personal commitment before the team continues.
Drop the topic because people disagree about the words.
responses: A clear explanation keeps the focus on the work. It also treats Dana’s question as a normal part of planning.
Questioning someone’s commitment moves attention from the task to the person. It does not answer the question about meaning.
Avoiding the topic leaves the actual concern about the meeting unresolved.

lessons.transfer: Using the practice meeting or a task in your own role, turn one broad statement into a task, a concern and a question the team can check. You do not need to describe any personal experience.

move.control: You can explain a term and invite a practical question about the work.
move.failure: Words become labels for people or a substitute for evidence.
move.next: Write one concrete question about a meeting, notice or form you handle.

lessons.title: Inclusion as belonging: who is present and whose input counts
lessons.summary: Separate who attends from whose input can shape the decision.
lessons.objective: Distinguish attendance from inclusion as belonging and real influence on the work.
objectives: Distinguish attendance from inclusion as belonging and real influence on the work.
Trace how a comment travels from invitation to decision.
Describe input without asking anyone to speak for a group.
takeaways: Attendance alone does not show that input could matter.
Inclusion needs a fair route for contributions and an explained result.
No one should have to share personal history or represent a whole group to take part.
lessons.statement: Look at the route a contribution travels, not only the list of who came.

image.caption: Two colleagues point to a line in a printed document they are reviewing together.

intro.heading: Belonging shows up in how the process works
intro.body:
The DHS Equity Policy describes inclusion in terms of the value of people’s contributions and their sense of belonging. In plain words, people belong in a process when they can take part on fair terms and their input can make a difference. A full room is a good start. It does not show by itself that anyone was heard.

In the practice case, Rosa’s meeting draws county workers, advocates, people who receive the notice and several interpreters. The agenda gives most of the time to a presentation. Written comments are read after the draft has already gone to print. The attendance list looks broad, but the process gives most participants no way to shape the notice.

Ask how the contribution route works. When do materials arrive? Which ways of responding can people use? Who reads the input, and what can still change? Do not ask participants to tell personal stories or to speak for everyone who shares a trait. A person can raise a specific concern about the notice without representing a whole community.

Inclusion does not mean every idea is adopted. Input may improve the draft, support keeping it, or point to a problem the team cannot solve yet. Explain which happened and why. A written account of what changed, and what did not, shows people that taking part was worth their time. The same open route applies to every participant.

lessons.keyStatement: People belong in a process when they can take part on fair terms and see what their input did.

flashcards.back: In the DHS Equity Policy, valued contributions and a sense of belonging. It depends on how people can take part, not only on a head count.
Being able to take part on fair terms, be heard and be treated as a full member of the group.
The path input takes from the invitation to the person deciding, including timing and ways to respond.
How input can affect a decision, including the reasons given and the questions left open.

items.title: Timing
items.body: Materials that arrive after the discussion cannot shape it. Check when each group received the draft notice and the agenda. Send the same materials to everyone at the same time, in formats and languages they can use.

items.title: Methods
items.body: Some people speak up in the room. Others write after they have time to think, or use an interpreter, captioning or a phone line. Offer more than one method to everyone so input does not depend on a single style.

items.title: Follow-through
items.body: Tell participants what changed, what did not and why. A short summary sent to all participants closes the loop. It also lets people correct the record if their point was misunderstood.

tabs.heading: Three views of the same meeting

tabs.label: Attendance
tabs.body: The sign-in sheet shows who came. That is useful information. It cannot show whether anyone could read the materials or reach the decision.

tabs.label: Participation
tabs.body: The agenda, the comment methods and the interpreter plan show whether people could take part. These are conditions the team controls and can improve.

tabs.label: Influence
tabs.body: The revision record shows whether input reached Rosa before the draft closed and what she did with it. This is where belonging becomes visible in the work.

check.question: The sign-in sheet shows a broad mix of attendees, but written comments were read after the draft was printed. What does this show?
check.correct: Attendance was broad, but the route for input to shape the draft was closed.
wrong: The meeting was inclusive because many kinds of people attended.
People who wrote comments should have spoken up in the room instead.
The team should ask attendees to share personal stories next time.
check.feedbackCorrect: Attendance and influence are different questions. The timing of the comment review kept input from reaching the decision.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A broad sign-in sheet does not show that input could matter, and written comments are a valid method. Personal stories are not the missing piece. The gap is in the timing of the review.

items.text: Forty people signed in.
Staff from six counties attended.
Interpreters were booked for Spanish, Somali and Hmong.
People could comment by phone, by email or in the room.
Two comments led Rosa to rewrite the deadline section.
A summary told all participants what changed and why.

lessons.next: Next, look at three words that are often confused: difference, disparity and equity.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The meeting had broad attendance, but only comments made during the presentation reached the draft before it was finalized.
scenario.prompt: What should the team look at first?
options: The timing and methods for input, alongside who attended.
Which attendees should be asked to share personal experiences next time.
Whether a group photo from the meeting shows that it went well.
responses: This finds the gap between being present and being able to shape the notice. The team can fix it for everyone.
Personal disclosure is not the missing route, and no one should be asked to speak for a group.
A photo shows who was there. It cannot show how input was handled.

lessons.transfer: Using the practice meeting or a process in your own role, describe one attendance detail, one participation condition and one way input could reach the decision.

move.control: You can make the route for input and the reasons for decisions clear.
move.failure: A broad attendance list is mistaken for a process where everyone’s input could matter.
move.next: Trace one comment from invitation to decision in a meeting you plan or attend.

lessons.title: Difference, disparity and equity: what a gap can tell you
lessons.summary: Read a difference in results carefully before naming its cause.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a recorded difference, a disparity and equity as the DHS Equity Policy uses the term.
objectives: Distinguish a recorded difference, a disparity and equity as the DHS Equity Policy uses the term.
Describe a gap without assigning a motive or a cause too early.
Name the evidence needed to explain a difference.
takeaways: A difference is an observation; it is not yet an explanation.
The DHS Equity Policy defines disparity and equity in specific ways.
Trace the process step by step to find where a gap begins.
lessons.statement: Describe the gap first. Then find out where in the process it begins.

image.caption: Two colleagues point to a line in a printed document they are reviewing together.

intro.heading: A number starts a question
intro.body:
A difference is a plain observation: two recorded results are not the same. The DHS Equity Policy uses disparity in a narrower way. It means systematic poorer outcomes for a group that are not explained by that group’s needs, eligibility or preferences. The policy describes equity as ongoing work to examine and address barriers, power, access, opportunities and outcomes. Both definitions require looking at the pattern and its context.

In the practice case, Rosa’s team finds that renewal forms come back late more often from one county than from others. That is a documented difference. Tracing the process shows that the county received the translated notice two weeks after the English version. The team can now test a specific explanation: the delay may have shortened the time readers had to respond.

Do not jump from a gap to a motive, or assume one cause explains every difference. A result can come from timing, mailing, reading level, staffing or a rule that lands harder on some people. Ask what the process does, who carries its burdens, what the people affected say and which evidence supports an explanation. Some questions will stay open. Write down the limit instead of filling it with a guess.

Civil rights law matters here too. Title VI bars discrimination based on race, color or national origin in federally funded programs. In December 2025 and July 2026, the federal Departments of Justice and of Health and Human Services removed the disparate-impact provisions from their Title VI regulations. The Justice Department noted that data on unequal outcomes can still help show intentional discrimination. The DHS Equity Policy still asks staff to examine disparities. Formal legal questions belong to the person or area responsible.

inThisLesson: Use the DHS definitions of disparity and equity.
Record what the evidence cannot show.
lessons.keyStatement: A gap is a reason to look closer, not a finished explanation.

flashcards.back: A plain observation that two recorded results are not the same.
In the DHS Equity Policy, systematic poorer outcomes for a group that are not explained by the group’s needs, eligibility or preferences.
As the DHS Equity Policy uses it: ongoing work to examine and address barriers, power, access, opportunities and outcomes.
A plain statement of what the available information cannot show.

items.title: Describe before explaining
items.body: Write the observation in plain terms: which result, which groups, which period and which source. Keep it separate from any explanation until the evidence supports one.

items.title: Trace the process
items.body: List each step from mailing to processing. Check where timing, format, language or rules differ. A step-by-step trace often finds a fixable cause that a summary number hides.

items.title: Measure and revisit
items.body: If the team changes a step, decide in advance which result it will watch and when. Look again after the change. A second look shows whether the fix helped the people it was meant to help.

tabs.heading: Three ways to describe the same finding

tabs.label: Observation
tabs.body: “Forms from one county came back late more often this quarter.” This is accurate and useful. It does not yet say why.

tabs.label: Supported explanation
tabs.body: “That county received the translated notice two weeks later than the English version, which shortened the time to respond.” This links the gap to a documented step the team can fix.

tabs.label: Unsupported claim
tabs.body: “People in that county do not take deadlines seriously.” This replaces evidence with a stereotype and points the team away from the cause it can change.

check.question: Late renewals are higher in one county. What should the team do first?
check.correct: Describe the difference, trace the process for that county and name the evidence needed to explain it.
wrong: Conclude that staff in that county are treating people unfairly.
Assume a cultural reason without checking the process.
Set the figures aside because the cause is uncertain.
check.feedbackCorrect: The trace keeps the observation useful while avoiding unsupported claims about motive or culture. It points to a cause the team can test.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A gap does not prove a motive or a cultural cause, and uncertainty is not a reason to discard data. Describe the gap, trace the steps and state what the evidence can and cannot show.

sorting.heading: Observation, supported explanation or unsupported claim?

items.text: Late returns rose in one county this quarter.
Processing took longer in that county than in the others.
The translated notice arrived two weeks late, and late returns were concentrated among its readers.
After phone reminders were added for every reader, on-time returns in that county matched the others.
People in that county do not care about deadlines.
The gap proves a staff member meant to treat people unfairly.

lessons.next: Next, separate two routes to access: planning for everyone and responding to an individual request.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Staff see different on-time rates between counties and want to announce the cause before checking how the notices were mailed.
options: Report the difference, trace the mailing process and state what evidence an explanation needs.
Choose a cultural explanation that seems to fit.
Hold back the figures until there is no uncertainty.
responses: This keeps the finding useful and avoids claims the evidence cannot support. It also points to a step the team can fix.
A cultural explanation without evidence is a stereotype. It can hide a fixable process problem.
Uncertainty can be stated honestly while the team keeps checking. Holding data back can delay a fix.

lessons.transfer: Using the practice case or a report you use in your own role, write one observed difference, one process step that might explain it and one thing the evidence cannot yet show.

move.control: You can describe a gap accurately and keep uncertainty visible.
move.failure: An observation becomes a conclusion about people that the evidence does not support.
move.next: Trace one process step by step before explaining a difference you see in your work.

lessons.title: Access and accommodation: two routes to the same goal
lessons.summary: Tell general access planning apart from an individual accommodation request.
lessons.objective: Distinguish general access from individual accommodation and the route each one takes.
objectives: Distinguish general access from individual accommodation and the route each one takes.
Match a public-service communication need to the right process.
Route an employee’s request to the employment accommodation process.
takeaways: Access is planned for everyone; accommodation responds to one person’s request.
Public services and employment have separate processes.
Ask what works for the person rather than assigning an aid by category.
lessons.statement: Plan for broad access, and still respond to each individual request.

image.caption: Two colleagues point to a line in a printed document they are reviewing together.

intro.heading: Two routes, one goal
intro.body:
Access means people can use a place, document, service or meeting. Teams plan for access before anyone asks, for example by making a notice readable with a screen reader and booking captioning. Accommodation is an individual change for one person with a disability. In employment it follows the Minnesota Management and Budget reasonable accommodation policy. In public services, the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 require reasonable changes to policies and effective communication.

In the practice case, the meeting packet includes a scanned image of the notice that a screen reader cannot read. The team fixes the packet through its usual document process. Separately, Dana, a team member, asks for a change in how a training is delivered because of a medical condition. Fixing the packet does not answer Dana’s request. Her request goes through the employment accommodation process.

For public communication, the nature, length and complexity of the exchange matter, and so does the method the person usually uses. Large print, accessible electronic text, captioning or a qualified sign language interpreter meet different needs. Ask the person what works for them. Do not assign an aid only from a category such as deaf or blind, or assume a written note works for a complex conversation.

Under the state policy, an employee does not need special words to ask. The person who receives the request promptly passes it to the right decision maker and explains who that is. Supervisors do not ask for medical information or documentation; any appropriate request comes from the agency’s Americans with Disabilities Act coordinator. Keep the details private and share only what others need to know.

inThisLesson: Separate the public and employment routes.
lessons.keyStatement: Good access planning removes barriers for many people; it does not replace one person’s request.

flashcards.back: People can use a place, document, service or meeting. Teams plan for it before anyone has to ask.
An individual change for a person with a disability, handled through the employment process or the public-service process that applies.
A public-service duty under the Americans with Disabilities Act, shaped by the task, its complexity and the person’s usual method.
The agency role that coordinates employment accommodation and handles any appropriate request for medical information.

items.title: General access
items.body: Fix barriers in materials and spaces for everyone. Use accessible documents, captions, clear signs and more than one way to respond. This work does not wait for a request.

items.title: Public-service request
items.body: When a person receiving services asks for a change or a communication aid, use the program’s process. Ask what method works for them and arrange qualified help.

items.title: Employment request
items.body: When an employee or applicant asks for a change because of a medical condition, start the employment accommodation process promptly. Do not ask for a diagnosis. Keep the details private.

tabs.label: Meeting packet
tabs.body: The scanned notice cannot be read with a screen reader. The team replaces it with accessible text. This improves the packet for everyone who uses assistive technology.

tabs.label: Person attending
tabs.body: A person who is hard of hearing asks for captioning at the meeting. The team asks what works best for them and arranges it through the program’s process.

tabs.label: Employee
tabs.body: Dana asks for a change to a training format. Her supervisor starts the employment accommodation process and does not ask about her diagnosis.

check.question: The team fixed the meeting packet. Dana then asks for a training change because of a medical condition. What should happen?
check.correct: Start the employment accommodation process for Dana’s request, separate from the packet fix.
wrong: Tell Dana the packet fix already covers access needs.
Ask Dana to explain her diagnosis to her supervisor first.
Wait until several employees ask for the same change.
check.feedbackCorrect: The packet fix and Dana’s request are different matters with different routes. Her request is handled individually and privately.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A general fix does not answer an individual request, and supervisors do not collect medical information. Each request is handled on its own, promptly, through the employment process.

sorting.heading: General access, public-service request or employment request?

items.text: Replace a scanned notice with accessible text.
Add captions to the recorded meeting video.
A person attending asks for a sign language interpreter.
A person receiving services asks to get notices in large print.
An employee asks for a different training format because of a medical condition.
An applicant asks for extra time on a written test because of a disability.

lessons.next: Next, connect culture, intercultural skill and language access to civil rights duties.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: After the packet repair, a team member suggests the team can set aside Dana’s separate request for a training change.
options: Keep Dana’s request in the employment accommodation process and respond to it on its own.
Ask Dana to show her supervisor proof of her diagnosis.
Tell Dana the repaired packet meets every access need.
responses: The packet repair and Dana’s request can need different actions. Handling each through its own route protects Dana’s rights and privacy.
Medical information is handled through the employment process, not collected by a supervisor.
One repaired document cannot show that every individual need is met.

lessons.transfer: Using the practice case or a task in your own role, sort two access needs by setting, the route each one takes and the information that should stay private.

move.control: You can tell general access from an individual request and use the right route.
move.failure: Different access needs are merged into one route, or an aid is assigned from a category without asking the person.
move.next: Check one document or meeting you prepare for screen reader access and a clear way to request help.

lessons.title: Connect intercultural learning and civil rights to practice
lessons.summary: Use culture, intercultural skill and language access to make a process work for everyone.
lessons.objective: Explain culture, intercultural skill and language access and connect them to civil rights duties.
objectives: Explain culture, intercultural skill and language access and connect them to civil rights duties.
Check an assumption about communication without assigning a group a fixed style.
Plan language access as a civil rights duty, not a favor.
takeaways: Culture is learned and shared, and people within any group vary widely.
Intercultural skill means noticing your own default and adapting the process.
Language access is a civil rights duty tied to national origin.
lessons.statement: Notice the default, then adjust the process so it works for everyone.

image.caption: Two colleagues point to a line in a printed document they are reviewing together.

intro.heading: Culture shapes the default; civil rights set the floor
intro.body:
Culture is a set of learned, shared patterns of communication, customs, beliefs and values. The National CLAS Standards describe culture this broadly, and every group includes wide individual variety. Intercultural skill is the ability to notice your own learned habits, shift perspective and adapt how you work across differences and commonalities. The DHS Equity Policy calls this intercultural competence. Learning a fact about a group is a start; it does not by itself build the skill.

In the practice meeting, the team expected objections to be raised out loud during the presentation. Malik points out that some people prefer to respond in writing after they have read the notice and talked with family. The team does not need to assign any group a fixed style. It can offer every participant a written option and a phone option with a clear deadline. Some differences come from access, role or preparation rather than culture, so check before assuming.

Language access is where intercultural learning meets a civil rights duty. Title VI bars discrimination based on national origin in federally funded programs. DHS provides free language help so people with limited English can understand and use its services. For Rosa’s notice, that means translated versions, the DHS language block telling readers how to get help, and qualified interpreters at the meeting. Avoid relying on family members, especially children, to interpret important information.

Keep the boundaries clear. Course activities do not measure or record anyone’s intercultural orientation. Describe the process change and its results, not personal labels. Language help and the written option are open to everyone who needs them. They do not give anyone a preference; they make the same service usable.

inThisLesson: Plan language access as a civil rights duty.
lessons.keyStatement: Adapting a process so it works for more people is a skill; providing language access is a duty.

flashcards.back: Learned, shared patterns of communication, customs, beliefs and values. People within any group vary widely.
The ability to notice your own learned habits, shift perspective and adapt your approach across differences and commonalities.
Free, qualified help so people with limited English can understand and use a program, including translation and interpreters.
A person who interprets accurately and impartially between languages, including sign language, using any specialized terms the task needs.

items.title: Check the default
items.body: Ask which habits the process takes for granted: speaking up in the moment, reading English, attending in person, answering by a set date. Each default works for some people and not for others.

items.title: Adapt for everyone
items.body: Add options that any participant can use, such as written comments, phone input and more time to read. This keeps one standard while removing barriers.

items.title: Meet the language duty
items.body: Plan translation and interpreters early, include the DHS language block, and check that translated materials reach readers at the same time as English materials.

tabs.label: Assumption
tabs.body: “People who disagree will say so in the meeting.” This treats one communication habit as the rule everyone is measured against.

tabs.label: Check
tabs.body: “Let us ask people who receive the notice how they prefer to respond, and offer more than one way.” This tests the assumption without labeling anyone.

tabs.label: Duty
tabs.body: “Send the Somali and Spanish versions with the English version and book interpreters.” This plans for language access, a civil rights duty under Title VI.

check.question: Few objections were raised aloud at the meeting. What is the best next step?
check.correct: Offer every participant written and phone options with a clear deadline, and ask people who receive the notice what works.
wrong: Conclude that participants from some cultures do not like to disagree.
Record each employee’s intercultural stage based on who suggested the new options.
Treat the quiet as agreement with the draft.
check.feedbackCorrect: This checks the assumption and opens more routes for everyone without assigning anyone a fixed style.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Silence can have many causes, and a cultural label can become a stereotype. Course activities also do not assess anyone’s orientation. Adding options and asking the readers tests the assumption directly.

sorting.heading: Assumption, check or civil rights duty?

items.text: Everyone who disagrees will speak up in the meeting.
Readers will understand the notice if it is in English.
Ask three people who receive the notice to explain it back in their own words.
Offer a written option to everyone and see who uses it.
Provide free language help to people with limited English.
Do not deny or delay a service because of a person’s national origin.

lessons.next: Next, use all the terms together in a plain-language note that leads to action.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The team adds written and phone comment options. A manager wants to record each staff member’s intercultural stage based on who suggested the change.
scenario.prompt: What should the record describe instead?
options: The process change, who it was offered to and what happened, without personal labels.
A score for each staff member based on their ideas in the meeting.
A note that people who preferred speaking aloud have less intercultural skill.
responses: The record shows the useful work and keeps personal assessments out of it.
Meeting ideas are not an assessment, and scoring them would label staff without a basis.
A preference for one method says nothing reliable about a person’s skill.

lessons.transfer: Using the practice case or a process in your own role, name one habit the process takes for granted, one option that would work for more people and one language access step.

move.control: You can notice a default and adjust a process so it works for more people.
move.failure: Concepts become labels for people, or language access is treated as optional.
move.next: Check that one notice or meeting you handle includes the DHS language block and a way to request an interpreter.

lessons.title: Use the terms together: a plain-language note that leads to action
lessons.summary: Turn the terms into a clear note, test it with readers and follow through.
lessons.objective: Write a plain-language note that names a task, a concern, the evidence, a limit and the person or area responsible for the next step.

lessons.statement: Write it so the reader can act on it, then check that they can.

intro.heading: From words to follow-through
intro.body:
Plain language is writing that the intended reader can find, understand and use the first time. It is a practical way to give everyone fair access to information. Minnesota Executive Order 14-07 directs state agencies to use plain language. The best test is simple: ask people who receive the notice to explain it back in their own words.

For Rosa’s team, “make the meeting more inclusive” becomes a clear note. Send the translated notice with the English version, offer written and phone comments to everyone, and make sure comments reach Rosa before the draft closes. A separate note covers the scanned document that needs an accessible version. Each note names who is responsible and when the team will check the result.

Person-centered practice keeps the focus on the people the notice affects. It means planning services around what matters to each person, their choices and the support they need, with informed choice. Federal rules require person-centered planning in home and community-based services. Minnesota’s Olmstead Plan rests on the same ideas of choice and the most integrated setting. For a notice, that means asking readers what they need in order to act, not guessing.

Keep the limits honest. A plain-language note can say what one test showed and what still needs review. For actual decisions, use the State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit and other required procedures. A glossary, practice note or finished course does not replace those duties. Write down how input shaped a changed or unchanged choice, and the reasons.

inThisLesson: Define plain language and person-centered practice.
Turn a broad goal into a clear note.
Name the next step and who owns it.
lessons.keyStatement: A clear note names the task, the evidence, the limit and who acts next.

flashcards.back: Writing the intended reader can find, understand and use the first time.
Planning services around what matters to the person, their choices and the support they need, with informed choice.
An action assigned to the person or area with the authority to take it, with a date to check the result.
Asking people who receive a document to explain it back, to check that it works before it goes out widely.

items.title: Name the task and concern
items.body: Say what the work is and what may be getting in the way. Use a term only if it helps, and explain it in a few words.

items.title: Show the evidence and the limit
items.body: State what was observed and how. Say what the evidence cannot show yet. This keeps the note honest and useful.

items.title: Assign and revisit
items.body: Name the person or area responsible and a date to look at the result. Measure the same thing again after the change.

tabs.label: Vague
tabs.body: “We will strengthen inclusion and access.” This sounds positive but gives no task, no owner and no way to check.

tabs.label: Clear
tabs.body: “Starting next month, send translated notices with the English version. Rosa’s team will compare on-time returns by county after one quarter.” This names a task, an owner and a measure.

tabs.label: Overclaimed
tabs.body: “The notice is now fully accessible and fair for everyone.” This claims more than one test or one change can show.

check.question: Which note best follows through on the practice meeting?
check.correct: Send translated notices with the English version, offer phone and written comments to all, and review on-time returns by county next quarter.
wrong: Our team is committed to inclusion and will keep it in mind.
The notice now meets every requirement because staff finished this course.
No note is needed because some questions remain open.
check.feedbackCorrect: This note names specific tasks, applies them to everyone and sets a measure to revisit.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A commitment without a task cannot be checked, finishing a course does not meet a legal requirement, and open questions can be stated in the note. A clear note names the task, the owner and the check.

items.text: Three readers explained the notice back correctly; two misread the deadline, so we are rewriting that line.
Rosa’s team will compare on-time returns by county in March.
We value everyone’s voice.
We will be more welcoming.
Completing this course shows our unit is compliant.
One fix made the notice work for everyone.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to write your own note, and choose a related course to continue.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: After learning the terms, a team wants to publish a statement that its notice process is now fully fair and accessible.
options: A plain note on what changed, what a reader test showed and which reviews are still needed.
A longer statement with more technical terms and no added evidence.
No statement at all until every question is settled.
responses: This shows real progress and keeps the remaining duties visible to the people responsible.
Technical terms cannot supply missing evidence or authority.
A clear account can be shared while its limits are stated.

lessons.transfer: Using the practice case or a notice in your own role, write a short plain-language note with the task, the term, the evidence, one limit, the responsible next step and a date to check the result.

move.control: You can turn a concern into a clear, checkable note.
move.failure: Learning the terms is mistaken for completing a required analysis or proving a result.
move.next: Ask two or three people who receive a notice you send to explain it back, and fix the parts they misread.

jobAid.subtitle: Use each term to clarify the task, the evidence and who acts next.
remember: Attendance, participation and influence are different questions.
A difference in results is an observation, not its own explanation.
General access and an individual accommodation can need different routes.

sections.heading: Explain the meaning
items: Name the task and the term that applies.
Ask which part of the process the concern describes.
Invite clarification without judging anyone’s commitment or motive.

sections.heading: Check the evidence
items: Separate attendance from influence, and an observation from its cause.
Trace the process step by step before explaining a gap.
Ask people who receive a notice to explain it back in their own words.

sections.heading: Use the right route
items: Send employment accommodation requests to the employment process, and keep medical details private.
Plan language access and accessible formats before anyone has to ask.
Apply the same criteria and options to everyone, and do not infer or record anyone’s intercultural orientation.

sections.heading: Communicate the result
items: State what the evidence supports and what it cannot show.
Name the person or area responsible and a date to check the result.
Do not treat a glossary or course completion as proof of compliance or results.
